note.text: An argument offers claims as reasons to accept another claim. It need not be a quarrel or a successful proof. Deductive reasoning aims at a conclusion that cannot be false if its premises are true. Inductive reasoning supports a conclusion with a degree of confidence instead. An explanation can give a cause for an event already accepted, rather than evidence that it occurred. Context determines the intended purpose. Evaluating the inference differs from checking whether its premises are actually true.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to distinguish an offered inference from description or explanation and assess its intended strength. Builds on: Form Four statements, conditions and logical form. Leads to: identifying premises, conclusions and indicators.

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original fictional rule: every reading-club voter holds a badge. Bih is a reading-club voter. Therefore Bih holds a badge. The stated premises support that conclusion. Reversing the rule would not establish that every badge holder votes. By contrast, Bih arrived late because the path was blocked may explain an accepted arrival, depending on context.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Identify the claim the speaker wants accepted and the offered reasons. Ask whether the intended support is necessary or probable. For an explanation, check whether the event is already accepted. Then test the support separately from checking real-world facts.

cards.idea: Read the whole example before identifying its function.
example: The badge rule and Bih’s voting status are reasons for her badge status.
The voter rule and Bih’s voter status entail her badge status.
Past club meetings suggest the next may also be busy.
The blocked path explains an arrival already accepted as late.

cards.idea: A correction must preserve scope, terms and assumptions.
example: An argument must be an angry disagreement. Correction: Reasons can be offered calmly.
Every deductive attempt is automatically valid. Correction: An aim can fail; the actual inference must be checked.
A repeated observation guarantees every future outcome. Correction: Such support can leave room for exceptions.
The word because always makes a passage a proof of its conclusion. Correction: Because can introduce a cause explaining an accepted event.

pick.q: Every club voter holds a badge; Bih is a voter; so she holds a badge. What support is intended?
w: An assertion that badges cause every vote.
e: No quarrel is described.
The claims are offered as reasons.
The rule does not express that causal claim.
pick.y: The conclusion is required if the stated premises hold.

pick.q: Several earlier meetings were busy, so the next will probably be busy. What is the intended strength?
e: The wording is probable.
A future claim is offered.
No exact negation is asserted.
pick.y: Earlier observations support an expectation without necessity.

pick.q: We already know the door closed. The speaker says it closed because a gust pushed it. What is the stated purpose?
w: Prove an event no one yet accepts.
Define every door as a gust.
Give a conclusion indicator with no cause.
e: The event is explicitly accepted.
The words do not define doors.
A cause is offered.
pick.y: The context supplies the explanatory purpose.

pick.q: All club voters have badges. Ayuk has a badge. Therefore Ayuk is a voter. What is the problem?
pick.r: The premises leave open badge holders who are not voters.
w: The conclusion follows merely because it is last.
The first premise says all badge holders vote.
e: Position does not establish support.
That reverses the stated rule.
The final claim is a conclusion.
